metadata.title: AI Literacy
metadata.prerequisite: None. Assumes basic computer and web skills only — browser, email, and file management. No programming and no math beyond arithmetic.

meetingSchedule.modality: Hybrid: an 80-minute live Zoom session each Monday, 5:30-6:50 PM, plus about 100 minutes of structured asynchronous work during the week. No on-campus meeting.
meetingSchedule.zoomLinkHtml: Join the Monday class session on Zoom

description.catalog: This course provides students from all disciplines with essential AI literacy skills needed to navigate an AI-integrated world. Students will develop a foundational understanding of AI technologies, learn to interact responsibly with AI tools, critically evaluate ethical implications, and explore AI's societal impact across various fields. The course emphasizes hands-on experience with AI applications while fostering critical thinking about AI's role in personal, academic, and professional contexts.
description.expanded: AI is already part of how you study, work, and live — this course makes you fluent in it. You will get hands-on with real AI tools every week: learning how they work under the hood (no coding required), how to prompt them well, how to catch them being wrong or biased, and how to decide when using them is smart, ethical, or neither. You will leave with a portfolio of real work — prompts, analyses, a personal AI code of conduct, a policy recommendation — that shows you can work with AI thoughtfully in your own field, whatever that field is. Google Gemini is the baseline tool and comes free with your college Google Workspace account; nothing in this course requires you to pay for anything.

purpose.why: Every field you might enter is being reshaped by tools that produce confident, fluent, sometimes wrong answers. The skill that matters is not knowing which product is best this month — that changes faster than a semester does — but being able to look at any AI output and judge what it is worth. That is what this course builds, and it transfers: to your other classes, to your job, and to decisions you make about AI as a citizen.
purpose.beyond: Beyond tool skills, you will develop critical thinking about AI's role in society, learn to recognize bias and evaluate fairness, protect your own data and privacy, and write a personal code for responsible AI use that you revise as you learn. Every assessment in this course is open-resource by design and asks for work AI cannot do for you — analysis of your own tool sessions, reflections tied to class discussions, and application in your own field. This course models the academic integrity it teaches.

slos: Define AI terminology, identify types of machine learning, and explain how AI systems function.
Demonstrate effective and ethical use of AI technologies in academic and professional contexts.
Evaluate AI-generated content for accuracy, bias, and appropriateness using established criteria.
Critique AI applications using ethical frameworks and justify decisions about AI use and development.
Integrate AI concepts with field-specific knowledge and create solutions for discipline-specific challenges.
Design personal guidelines for responsible AI use and develop strategies for lifelong AI literacy.

aiPolicy.title: AI Policy for This Course
aiPolicy.approach: Open — AI use is expected and taught, with required disclosure
aiPolicy.scopeNote: This policy applies to CSC 141 only. Every course sets its own AI policy, and what is expected here may be prohibited in your English, history, or math class. Always check each instructor's syllabus. Nothing in this policy gives you permission to use AI in another course.
aiPolicy.summary: This is a course about AI, so you will use AI extensively — that is the coursework, not a loophole. Two rules make it work: disclose what the tool did, and do your own evaluating. Everything below follows from those two.
permitted: Use AI throughout the course. Brainstorming, drafting, summarizing, explaining a concept you did not follow in session, generating examples, comparing outputs across tools, translating something into plainer language, checking your own writing — all of it, on any assignment, unless a specific activity says otherwise.

Use whatever tool you like beyond the Gemini baseline. Demonstrations use Google Gemini so everyone sees the same screen, but once you are comfortable, your tool choices are your own. When an activity requires a particular tool, it will say so and explain why.
Use AI to help you study. Quiz yourself, ask for a different explanation, have it walk you through why an answer was wrong. Concept quizzes are open-resource and retake-friendly on purpose.

Generate material you will then analyze. Most module artifacts start with AI output you produced — a biased result, a weak citation, a set of three tool responses to the same prompt. Producing that material with AI is the assignment.
required: Disclose your AI use on every submission that involved it. One or two sentences: which tool and version, what you asked it to do, and what you changed or verified yourself. There is no penalty for disclosing — the disclosure is part of the work, and a missing one is what causes problems.
Verify anything factual before you rely on it. Open the citation. Follow the link. Confirm the number. A citation tells you where to check; it is not proof that anyone checked.
Keep your prompts and sessions. Several artifacts ask you to show your process, not just your result. Screenshots or exported transcripts are the easiest way.

Protect other people's information. Never enter your student ID, your grades, another student's work, or anyone's personal information into any AI tool. If an assignment seems to require it, it does not — ask me and I will give you the workaround. Tools on your personal accounts run under that company's terms, which you accept yourself.
aiPolicy.notPermittedHeading: The one hard line: you do the evaluating
notPermitted: Do not use AI to evaluate AI-generated content. When an assignment asks you to judge accuracy, detect bias, assess fairness, rate appropriateness, or check quality, that judgment must be yours. Do not paste an output into a second tool and ask it whether the first one was biased, accurate, or any good.
Do not use AI to write your reflections. Module reflections, the synthesis reflection, and your Personal AI Code are accounts of your own experience and thinking. A model cannot have had your week.

Do not let AI make the argument in your policy brief or your critique. You may use it to research, to check your reasoning, or to find the counterargument — but the position, and the justification for it, has to be yours.
Do not submit AI output as if you produced it. Undisclosed AI work that was supposed to be disclosed is an academic honesty matter under AP 5500.2, not a style problem.
aiPolicy.whyThisLine: Every one of this course's learning outcomes above the first is an evaluation or creation outcome — evaluating content for accuracy and bias, critiquing applications against ethical frameworks, designing your own guidelines. Outsourcing the evaluation outsources exactly the skill the course exists to build, and it is the skill that will still matter when today's tools are three generations obsolete. It is also the one thing on your transcript an employer cannot get from a subscription.
aiPolicy.consequences: Work that outsources the evaluation is graded on what it demonstrates, which is not much — it is a grading outcome, not a disciplinary one, and you will get the chance to redo it. Undisclosed AI use where disclosure was required, or submitting someone else's work as your own, falls under the College Academic Honesty Policy (AP 5500.2) and is handled accordingly.
aiPolicy.uncertainty: If you are not sure whether something is allowed, ask before you submit. Asking is always safe, it never counts against you, and in a course like this the question itself is usually worth class time.

schedule._rhythm: Class meets Mondays 5:30-6:50 PM on Zoom, so each session is primed by the PREVIOUS week's work. Monday session = discussion of last week + launch of this week. During the week = about 100 minutes of structured asynchronous work (activity or studio). By Sunday night = pre-work for next Monday. Weekly work is due Sunday 11:59 PM unless noted.

breakdown.description: Six signature artifacts, one per module, graded against a rubric as each module closes (40 + 60 + 50 + 60 + 60 + 50 = 320 pts). Each is hands-on application verifying that module's outcomes.

Six module reflections (15 pts each = 90 pts) plus the final assembly and synthesis reflection (70 pts) = 160 pts. Student-created and student-maintained: export each artifact and reflection at studio close and file it in your own portfolio.
Four low-stakes quizzes covering Modules 1-4 (30 pts each = 120 pts), delivered in the Canvas quiz system. Retake-friendly: best of 2 attempts, with any time limits managed by Canvas.
Weekly, credit/no credit, weeks 2-16 (8 pts each = 120 pts). This is the primer that makes the Monday discussions work. Week 1 has no pre-work by design.

80 pts. Choose one track. Portfolio track (week 17): a 4-5 minute highlight-reel walkthrough plus one live Q&A question. Topic track (weeks 5-14, instructor approval required): a short deep dive on any AI topic you want to go further on. Everyone submits the full portfolio either way.

scale.range: You may elect Pass/No Pass instead of a letter grade. Pass = 70% or higher. The election deadline is set by the college — see Important Semester Dates.

required: Zoom for the Monday class session, 5:30-6:50 PM Pacific: Join the CSC 141 Monday session. Sessions are recorded and posted in Canvas.
No textbook. All readings and interactive materials are provided through Canvas and the course app at no cost.
A computer with a current web browser, your Mendocino College email, and Canvas. A phone alone is not enough for most coursework.

Google Gemini — the baseline tool for this course. It comes free with your college Google Workspace account (@student.mendocino.edu); there is nothing to sign up for. Class demonstrations and walkthroughs use Gemini, so what is on your screen will match what is on the shared screen.
NotebookLM and Microsoft Copilot (web) — also free with your college login, used where comparing tools teaches something.

Nothing in this course requires you to pay for anything. Every activity can be completed on free tiers, and nearly all of them on your college account alone. You never need an account outside the college.
optional: Personal free tiers on your own account and your own terms: ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, DeepSeek, Perplexity, and others. Several assignments invite you to compare tools; those will say exactly what is required. If you use one of these you are agreeing to that company's terms yourself — never put your student ID, your grades, other students' work, or anyone's personal information into it.

Tool guides for each supported tool, linked from the course homepage: setup, interface, free-tier limits, what the tool does with your data, and what it is bad at. These are ungraded reference material and are never required reading — every graded concept is taught in the lessons themselves.

Tool guides carry an "accurate as of" date. AI products change faster than a semester does, so if what you see on screen does not match the guide, trust the screen and tell me. Noticing that gap is itself an AI-literacy skill.

workload.breakdown: 3 hrs in-class equivalent (80-min Monday Zoom session, 5:30-6:50 PM, plus about 100 min of structured asynchronous work) + 6 hrs out-of-class work on assignments, portfolio, and discussion pre-work
workload.notes: This matches the Course Outline of Record: 51 in-class contact hours and 102 out-of-class hours across 17 weeks, for 153 total student learning hours. Studio weeks (3, 6, 8, 11, 14, 16) sit at the top of that range. Thanksgiving week (15) is deliberately light at about 1.5 hours total. If you are consistently well over 9 hours, email me — that usually means an instruction is unclear rather than that you are behind.

policies.attendance: Come to the Monday sessions when you can — the discussion is the course, and it works because people arrive having done the previous week's material. Sessions are recorded and posted in Canvas. If work, caregiving, or illness keeps you from attending live, watch the recording and post to that week's discussion board; you earn the same credit and you will not lose participation points for a schedule you cannot control. As a hybrid course, regular weekly engagement in Canvas and the course app is what demonstrates attendance. If your internet access is unreliable, tell me in week 1 — every graded activity has a low-bandwidth path, and the library loans laptops and hotspots.
policies.lateWork: Module artifacts and reflections have a standing 48-hour grace window with no penalty and no need to ask. After that, contact me before the deadline if you can, or as soon as you are able if you cannot — I would much rather adjust a deadline than lose you. Discussion pre-work is credit/no credit and must be submitted before its Monday session to serve its purpose, so it is not accepted late; the two lowest pre-work scores are dropped to absorb the weeks life gets in the way. Concept quizzes are open for a window in Canvas with best-of-2 attempts and are not reopened afterward. The final portfolio and synthesis reflection cannot be accepted after Thursday 12/10/2026 because grades are due. This course-specific policy replaces the general late-submission statement shown under Policies & Resources.
policies.makeupExams: There are no exams in this course — no midterm, no final. Every assessment is open-resource by design and asks you to demonstrate the outcome through your own work: analysis of your own tool sessions, reflections tied to our discussions, and application in your own field. If you miss an oral presentation slot for a documented emergency, contact me within 48 hours and we will schedule a replacement.
policies.academicIntegrity:
See the AI Policy for This Course under Policies & Resources for the full statement on how AI may and may not be used in CSC 141 — it is the governing policy for this course and it is detailed, because the subject demands it. In short: use AI extensively and disclose it, but do your own evaluating.

Beyond AI, ordinary academic honesty applies. All work you submit must be your own effort, properly attributed. Academic dishonesty — cheating, plagiarism, fabrication, or submitting another person's work as yours — falls under the College Academic Honesty Policy (AP 5500.2) and may result in a failing grade on the assignment or in the course, plus referral for disciplinary action. If you are ever unsure whether something crosses a line, ask me before you submit. Asking is always safe.
